title: Bài sưu tầm 105 - Passage 1: Saffron: The Golden Threads of History
passageHtml:
READING PASSAGE 1 — TEST 105

Saffron: The Golden Threads of History

Paragraph 1. Renowned for its distinctive, honeyed aroma, vibrant golden hue, and subtle, bitter taste, saffron is universally acknowledged as the most expensive culinary spice in the world. Derived from the dried stigmas of the lilac-flowered saffron crocus (Crocus sativus), this prized botanical commodity has been cultivated for over four millennia across the Mediterranean basin and Western Asia. Throughout human history, civilizations have revered saffron not merely as a seasoning for banquet feasts, but as a prestigious fabric dye, an aphrodisiac, a sacred temple incense, and a therapeutic agent prescribed to remedy physical ailments ranging from ocular disorders to respiratory fevers.

Paragraph 2. The botanical origin of the saffron crocus presents a biological puzzle. Unlike its wild ancestors, Crocus sativus is a genetically sterile triploid mutant. Because the plant cannot produce fertile seeds or cross-pollinate naturally, it is entirely incapable of reproducing in the wild. Its long-term evolutionary survival depends exclusively on human intervention. Propagation is carried out through vegetative cloning: farmers dig up mature underground storage bulbs, known as corms, split off the small daughter offshoots, and manually replant them into well-drained, semi-arid soil. Without this ongoing horticultural effort, the spice-yielding crocus would disappear from the planet within a few generations.

Paragraph 3. The staggering economic cost of saffron is dictated by its extraordinarily labour-intensive harvesting protocol. The plant flowers for an extremely brief window of approximately two to three weeks in late autumn. The delicate blooms must be gathered by hand at dawn, just as the petals begin to unfurl, to prevent direct, midday sunlight from bleaching the fragile chemical compounds responsible for its rich colour and flavor. Each flower produces precisely three slender, thread-like red stigmas attached to a central style. Because mechanical harvesters tear the fragile plant tissues and destroy the yield, workers must stoop over vast fields to hand-pick every individual bloom. It takes an astonishing 150,000 blossoms, requiring roughly forty hours of grueling manual labor, to produce a single dry kilogram of marketable saffron.

Paragraph 4. Once severed from the flowers, the fresh stigmas are subjected to a delicate drying regime. Saffron's distinctive sensory properties stem from three primary phytochemicals: crocin, which confers its vivid orange-yellow color; picrocrocin, which produces its characteristic bitterness; and safranal, an essential oil that releases its warm fragrance. Fresh stigmas possess little aroma; it is only through carefully regulated dehydration—traditionally performed by roasting the filaments over charcoal embers or spreading them on fine silk screens in heated drying rooms—that volatile aroma compounds develop. Over-drying scorches the filaments and degrades medicinal potency, while retaining excess moisture leaves the spice susceptible to fungal decay.

Paragraph 5. Because pure saffron routinely commands prices equivalent to silver or fine gemstones, fraudulent adulteration has plagued the spice trade since antiquity. Dishonest merchants frequently blended authentic threads with shredded beet fibers, dried marigold petals, or finely sliced turmeric roots. Others artificially increased the product's weight by spraying batches with salt water or coating the threads in mineral oil. In medieval Europe, the adulteration of saffron was considered a major economic crime against public health. Under the legendary Safranschau statutes implemented in fifteenth-century Nuremberg, municipal inspectors regularly audited trading houses, and merchants convicted of selling fraudulent saffron were condemned to public burning alongside their counterfeit wares. Today, advanced laboratory testing ensures spice purity, safeguarding an ancient agricultural legacy that remains virtually unchanged across thousands of years.

steps: Đoạn 2: "...evolutionary survival depends exclusively on human intervention."
Đoạn 3: "...prevent direct, midday sunlight from bleaching the fragile chemical compounds..."
Đoạn 3: "...produces precisely three slender, thread-like red stigmas..."
Đoạn 3: "Because mechanical harvesters tear the fragile plant tissues..."
Đoạn 4: "...retaining excess moisture leaves the spice susceptible to fungal decay."

q8.text: Cultivation of the saffron crocus first began in Northern Europe.

steps: Đoạn 1: Trồng trọt lần đầu ở Địa Trung Hải và Tây Á ("across the Mediterranean basin and Western Asia"), mâu thuẫn với "Northern Europe".

q9.text: The saffron plant blooms continuously for several months every year.

steps: Đoạn 3: Cây chỉ nở hoa trong một khoảng thời gian rất ngắn khoảng 2–3 tuần vào cuối thu ("extremely brief window of approximately two to three weeks in late autumn"), mâu thuẫn với "continuously for several months".

q10.text: Freshly picked saffron stigmas have a much stronger scent than dried ones.

steps: Đoạn 4: Nhụy hoa tươi hầu như không có mùi hương ("Fresh stigmas possess little aroma; it is only through... dehydration... that volatile aroma compounds develop") → mâu thuẫn trực tiếp.

q11.text: High temperatures during the drying process can reduce the medicinal strength of saffron.

steps: Đoạn 4: Sấy quá nóng làm cháy sợi và giảm dược tính ("Over-drying scorches the filaments and degrades medicinal potency").

q12.text: The city of Nuremberg hired inspectors from other countries to test saffron quality.

steps: Đoạn 5: Có nhắc đến thành phố Nuremberg có các thanh tra kiểm tra hàng quán ("municipal inspectors regularly audited trading houses"), nhưng bài đọc không đề cập họ có được thuê từ nước ngoài hay không.

q13.text: Merchants found guilty of faking saffron in medieval Nuremberg faced capital punishment.

steps: Đoạn 5: Thương lái bán nhụy hoa nghệ tây giả bị thiêu sống nơi công cộng ("...merchants convicted of selling fraudulent saffron were condemned to public burning") → án tử hình / capital punishment.
